title: CTET — Language II English | Grammar Tenses
description: Subject-wise test on Grammar Tenses (Language II English) for CTET. 30Q.
subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: My brother usually ______ to school by bus.

options.explanation: Incorrect because it doesn't match the third-person singular subject.
Correct because it matches the third-person singular subject and indicates a habitual action.
Incorrect because it's in the past tense and doesn't match the habitual action indicated by "usually".
Incorrect because it's in the present continuous tense and doesn't match the habitual action indicated by "usually".

questions.explanation: The adverb "usually" indicates a habitual action, which requires the simple present tense. For a third-person singular subject ("My brother"), the verb takes an "-es" ending.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Yesterday, I ______ an interesting documentary on wildlife.

options.explanation: Incorrect because it's in the base form and doesn't match the past tense indicated by "Yesterday".
Incorrect because it's in the present perfect tense and doesn't match the completed action in the past.
Correct because it matches the completed action in the past indicated by "Yesterday".
Incorrect because it's in the present continuous tense and doesn't match the completed action in the past.

questions.explanation: The time marker "Yesterday" clearly indicates a completed action in the past. Therefore, the simple past tense ("watched") is the correct choice.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Since she moved to the city, she ______ many new friends.

options.explanation: Incorrect because it's in the simple past tense and doesn't match the action that continues up to the present.
Correct because it matches the action that began in the past and continues up to the present.
Incorrect because it's in the simple present tense and doesn't match the action that began in the past.
Incorrect because it's in the present continuous tense and doesn't match the action that began in the past and continues up to the present.

questions.explanation: The word "since" indicates an action that began in the past (when she moved) and continues to have an effect or is still true up to the present. This situation requires the present perfect tense ("has made").
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: By the time we arrived at the station, the train ______ already ______.

options.explanation: Incorrect because it's in the present perfect tense and doesn't match the past actions.
Correct because it matches the action completed before another past action.
Incorrect because it's in the past continuous tense and doesn't match the action completed before another past action.
Incorrect because it's in the present continuous tense and doesn't match the past actions.

questions.explanation: This sentence describes two past actions. The train's departure happened before our arrival. To indicate an action completed before another past action, the past perfect tense ("had left") is used for the earlier event.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Don't call me between 7 and 8 PM tomorrow; I ______ dinner.

options.explanation: Incorrect because it's in the future perfect tense and doesn't match the ongoing action at a specific future time.
Correct because it matches the ongoing action at a specific future time.
Incorrect because it's in the present tense and doesn't match the future action.
Incorrect because it's in the present continuous tense and doesn't match the future action.

questions.explanation: The phrase "between 7 and 8 PM tomorrow" specifies a period in the future during which an action will be in progress. The future continuous tense ("will be having") is used to express an ongoing action at a specific future time.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: If it ______ tomorrow, we ______ the picnic.

options.explanation: Correct because it matches the Type 1 conditional sentence.
Incorrect because it's in the past tense and doesn't match the Type 1 conditional sentence.
Incorrect because it's in the future tense and doesn't match the Type 1 conditional sentence.
Incorrect because it's in the present continuous tense and doesn't match the Type 1 conditional sentence.

questions.explanation: This is a Type 1 conditional sentence, which describes a real or very probable situation in the future. The 'if' clause uses the simple present tense ("rains"), and the main clause uses the simple future tense ("will cancel").
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: The children ______ in the garden for two hours, so they are quite tired now.

options.explanation: Incorrect because it's in the simple past tense and doesn't match the action that continues up to the present.
Incorrect because it's in the present perfect tense and doesn't match the action that continues up to the present.
Correct because it matches the action that started in the past, continues up to the present, and has a visible result in the present.
Incorrect because it's in the present continuous tense and doesn't match the action that started in the past.

questions.explanation: The sentence indicates an action that started in the past ("for two hours"), continued up to the present, and has a visible result in the present ("they are quite tired now"). This situation requires the present perfect continuous tense ("have been playing").
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: She wished she ______ the opportunity to travel more when she was younger.

options.explanation: Incorrect because it's in the past tense and doesn't match the past counterfactual desire.
Incorrect because it's in the present perfect tense and doesn't match the past counterfactual desire.
Incorrect because it's in the conditional tense and doesn't match the past counterfactual desire.
Correct because it matches the past counterfactual desire.

questions.explanation: When "wish" is used to express regret about a past situation that did not happen or was different, the past perfect tense is used in the clause following "wish." Here, "had had" correctly expresses this past counterfactual desire.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: If I ______ more carefully, I ______ the accident yesterday.

options.explanation: Incorrect because it's in the simple past tense and doesn't match the Type 3 conditional sentence.
Correct because it matches the Type 3 conditional sentence.
Incorrect because it's in the past perfect tense and doesn't match the Type 3 conditional sentence.
Incorrect because it's in the simple past tense and doesn't match the Type 3 conditional sentence.

questions.explanation: This is a Type 3 conditional sentence, used to talk about hypothetical situations in the past and their hypothetical results. The 'if' clause requires the past perfect tense ("had driven"), and the main clause requires "would have + past participle" ("wouldn't have had").
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Look! The sun ______ brightly now.

options.explanation: Incorrect because it's in the base form and doesn't match the action happening at the exact moment of speaking.
Incorrect because it's in the simple present tense and doesn't match the action happening at the exact moment of speaking.
Correct because it matches the action happening at the exact moment of speaking.
Incorrect because it's in the past tense and doesn't match the action happening at the exact moment of speaking.

questions.explanation: The word "now" and the exclamation "Look!" indicate an action happening at the exact moment of speaking. This requires the present continuous tense ("is shining").
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: The Earth ______ around the Sun.

options.explanation: The verb 'moved' is in the Simple Past tense, which does not match the context of a universal truth.
The verb 'is moving' is in the Present Continuous tense, which implies an action in progress, not a general fact.
The verb 'moves' is in the Simple Present tense, which is used to express universal truths or general facts.
The verb 'has moved' is in the Present Perfect tense, which implies an action that started in the past and continues up to the present, not a general fact.

questions.explanation: This is a universal truth or a general fact, which is always expressed in the Simple Present tense.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Choose the correct form of the verb to complete the sentence: She usually _____ to school by bus.

options.explanation: Incorrect because 'go' is the base form of the verb and does not agree with the third-person singular subject 'She'.
Incorrect because 'going' is the present participle form and does not fit the simple present tense required here.
Correct because 'goes' is the simple present tense form of the verb for the third-person singular subject 'She'.
Incorrect because 'went' is the simple past tense and does not match the habitual action indicated by 'usually'.

questions.explanation: The adverb 'usually' indicates a habitual action, which requires the simple present tense. For a third-person singular subject ('She'), the verb takes an '-es' ending.
questions.hint: Think about the subject and the habitual nature of the action.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Identify the tense used in the following sentence: 'The sun rises in the east.'

options.explanation: Incorrect because the sentence does not refer to an action that happened in the past.
Incorrect because the sentence does not refer to an action that will happen in the future.
Incorrect because the sentence does not describe an action happening at the moment of speaking.
Correct because the sentence describes a universal truth using the simple present tense.

questions.explanation: The simple present tense is used to express universal truths, facts, and habitual actions. 'The sun rises in the east' is a universal truth.
questions.hint: Consider the nature of the statement—is it a fact or an ongoing action?
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Complete the sentence with the most appropriate tense: I _____ for two hours when you called me last night.

options.explanation: Correct because it uses the past perfect continuous tense to describe an action that continued for a duration before another past action.
Incorrect because 'have studied' is the present perfect tense and does not match the past context.
Incorrect because 'was studying' is the past continuous tense and does not emphasize the duration as clearly.
Incorrect because 'studied' is the simple past tense and does not indicate the duration of the action.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'for two hours' indicates a duration, and 'when you called me last night' indicates a specific point in the past. The past perfect continuous tense (had been studying) is used to describe an action that started in the past, continued for a duration, and was still ongoing or had just stopped at another point in the past.
questions.hint: Look for the duration and the specific past time mentioned in the sentence.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses the Present Perfect Tense?

options.explanation: Incorrect because it uses the simple past tense ('visited') and does not indicate a present relevance.
Incorrect because it uses the present continuous tense ('are playing') and does not fit the present perfect tense.

options.text: He has finished his homework already.
options.explanation: Correct because it uses the present perfect tense ('has finished') and 'already' indicates completion with present relevance.

options.text: We will go to the market tomorrow.
options.explanation: Incorrect because it uses the simple future tense ('will go') and does not fit the present perfect tense.

questions.explanation: The present perfect tense is used for actions that started in the past and continue to the present, or actions completed in the past but having a present relevance. Option C uses 'has finished' (present perfect) and 'already' which signifies completion with current relevance.
questions.hint: Look for the use of 'has/have' + past participle in the sentence.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: If it _____, we would have gone for a picnic.

options.explanation: Incorrect because it uses the simple past tense and does not fit the Third Conditional structure.
Incorrect because it uses the simple present tense and does not fit the Third Conditional structure.
Correct because it uses the past perfect tense ('hadn't rained') to fit the Third Conditional structure.
Incorrect because it uses the conditional form and does not fit the Third Conditional structure.

questions.explanation: This is an example of a Third Conditional sentence, which describes a hypothetical situation in the past and its hypothetical result. The structure for the Third Conditional is 'If + Past Perfect, Subject + would have + Past Participle.' Therefore, 'hadn't rained' is the correct choice.
questions.hint: Identify the type of conditional sentence and its structure.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: According to the schedule, the flight _____ at 3 PM.

options.explanation: Incorrect because while 'will arrive' can indicate future, 'arrives' is more standard for fixed schedules.
Incorrect because 'is arriving' is the present continuous tense and does not fit the context of a schedule.
Correct because the simple present tense is used for scheduled future events.
Incorrect because 'has arrived' is the present perfect tense and does not fit the context of a schedule.

questions.explanation: The simple present tense is often used to refer to scheduled future events (timetables, programs). The phrase 'According to the schedule' explicitly points to this usage, making 'arrives' the most appropriate choice.
questions.hint: Consider the context of schedules and timetables.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses the Past Perfect Continuous Tense?

options.text: He had been working on the project for five hours before he took a break.
options.explanation: Correct because it uses the past perfect continuous tense ('had been working') to describe an action that continued for a duration before another past action.

options.text: She has been living in London since 2010.
options.explanation: Incorrect because it uses the present perfect continuous tense ('has been living') and does not fit the past context.

options.text: They were playing football when it started to rain.
options.explanation: Incorrect because it uses the past continuous tense ('were playing') and does not fit the past perfect continuous tense.

options.text: I had finished my dinner by the time she arrived.
options.explanation: Incorrect because it uses the past perfect tense ('had finished') and does not fit the past perfect continuous tense.

questions.explanation: The past perfect continuous tense (had been + verb-ing) is used to indicate an action that started in the past, continued for a duration, and was in progress or had just finished at another point in the past. Option A perfectly fits this description.
questions.hint: Look for the structure 'had been + verb-ing' in the sentence.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: 'If I _____ a bird, I _____ fly.' Choose the correct pair of verbs to complete the conditional sentence.

options.explanation: Incorrect because 'am' is the present tense and does not fit the Second Conditional structure.
Incorrect because 'was' is not conventionally used for all subjects in the Second Conditional.
Correct because 'were' is used for all subjects in the Second Conditional, and 'would' is the correct modal verb.
Incorrect because it uses the Third Conditional structure and does not fit the Second Conditional.

questions.explanation: This is a Second Conditional sentence, used for hypothetical or unlikely situations in the present or future. The structure is 'If + Simple Past (often 'were' for all persons), Subject + would + base verb.' In this specific type of conditional (hypothetical), 'were' is conventionally used for all subjects, including 'I', making 'were, would' the correct pair.
questions.hint: Identify the type of conditional sentence and its structure.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Identify the sentence where the tense usage is incorrect.

options.text: By next month, I will have completed my novel.
options.explanation: Correct usage of the future perfect tense.

options.text: The child has been sleeping soundly for two hours now.
options.explanation: Correct usage of the present perfect continuous tense.

options.text: We lived in that house since 2005.
options.explanation: Incorrect because it uses the simple past tense ('lived') with 'since 2005,' which requires the present perfect tense.

options.text: She had already left when I reached her home.
options.explanation: Correct usage of the past perfect tense.

questions.explanation: Option C is incorrect. The phrase 'since 2005' indicates an action that began in the past and continues up to the present. This requires either the present perfect tense ('We have lived in that house since 2005') or the present perfect continuous tense ('We have been living in that house since 2005'). The simple past tense ('lived') implies the action is finished, which contradicts the 'since' clause.
questions.hint: Look for the use of 'since' and the tense required for actions continuing to the present.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Choose the correct option to complete the sentence: She _____ her studies before she got married.

options.explanation: Incorrect because 'completes' is the simple present tense and does not fit the past context.
Correct because it uses the past perfect tense ('had completed') to show an action that occurred before another past action.
Incorrect because 'has completed' is the present perfect tense and does not fit the past context.
Incorrect because 'will complete' is the simple future tense and does not fit the past context.

questions.explanation: The sentence describes two past actions: 'completing studies' and 'getting married.' The action of completing studies happened before the action of getting married. To show an action that occurred before another past action, the past perfect tense (had completed) is used.
questions.hint: Look for the sequence of past actions and the tense required to show the earlier action.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Which of the following sentences uses the correct tense form of the verb in parentheses?

options.text: She (go) to school every day when she was younger.
options.explanation: The verb should be in the simple past tense ('went') to describe a habitual action in the past.

options.text: She went to school every day when she was younger.
options.explanation: The simple past tense ('went') correctly describes a habitual action in the past.

questions.explanation: The sentence describes a habitual action in the past, so the simple past tense ('went') is correct.
questions.hint: Consider the time frame of the action described.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Identify the tense used in the following sentence: 'By next month, they will have completed their project.'

options.explanation: Simple future tense does not indicate completion before a future time.
Future continuous tense describes an action in progress at a future time, not completion.
Future perfect tense ('will have completed') indicates an action completed before a specified future time.

questions.explanation: The sentence indicates an action that will be completed before a specified future time ('by next month'), which is the definition of the future perfect tense.
questions.hint: Look for the phrase that indicates a future completion before another time.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Choose the correct option to fill in the blank: 'If I _____ (know) about the meeting, I would have attended it.'

options.explanation: The base form 'know' is incorrect for a third conditional sentence.
The simple past 'knew' is incorrect for a third conditional sentence.
The past perfect 'had known' correctly forms the third conditional sentence.

questions.explanation: The sentence is a third conditional, which requires the past perfect tense ('had known') to express a hypothetical situation in the past.
questions.hint: Third conditional sentences use 'had + past participle' in the if-clause.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: He has been working here since five years.
options.explanation: The preposition 'since' is used for specific points in time, not durations like 'five years'.

options.text: He works here since five years.
options.explanation: The simple present tense 'works' is incorrect for indicating a duration of time.

options.text: He has been working here for five years.
options.explanation: The present perfect continuous tense with 'for' correctly indicates a duration of time.

questions.explanation: The correct sentence uses the present perfect continuous tense ('has been working') with the preposition 'for' to indicate a duration of time.
questions.hint: Consider the correct use of 'since' vs. 'for' with present perfect continuous tense.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Select the sentence that correctly uses the past perfect tense.

options.text: She had finished her homework before she went out to play.
options.explanation: The past perfect tense ('had finished') correctly indicates an action completed before another past action.

options.text: She finished her homework before she went out to play.
options.explanation: The simple past tense 'finished' does not indicate an action completed before another past action.

options.text: She was finishing her homework before she went out to play.
options.explanation: The past continuous tense 'was finishing' does not indicate completion before another past action.

questions.explanation: The past perfect tense ('had finished') is used to indicate an action completed before another past action ('went out to play').
questions.hint: Look for the use of 'had + past participle' to indicate an action completed before another past action.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Identify the error in the following sentence: 'They has been waiting for the bus since morning.'

options.explanation: The subject 'They' is correct; the error lies in the verb.
The singular verb 'has' is incorrect for the plural subject 'They'; it should be 'have'.
The verb form 'waiting' is correct; the error lies in the auxiliary verb 'has'.

questions.explanation: The plural subject 'They' requires the plural verb 'have' instead of 'has' to agree in number.
questions.hint: Check subject-verb agreement for plural subjects.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Choose the correct transformation of the following sentence into the passive voice: 'The teacher is teaching the lesson.'

options.text: The lesson is taught by the teacher.
options.explanation: This is the simple present passive form, not the present continuous passive form.

options.text: The lesson was being taught by the teacher.
options.explanation: This uses the past continuous passive form, which does not match the original sentence's tense.

options.text: The lesson is being taught by the teacher.
options.explanation: This correctly transforms the present continuous active sentence into the passive voice.

questions.explanation: The original sentence is in the present continuous tense. Its passive form is 'The lesson is being taught by the teacher,' maintaining the tense and adding 'being' for the continuous aspect.
questions.hint: Convert the active sentence to passive by making the object the subject and using the appropriate form of 'be' + past participle.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Which of the following sentences correctly uses the future continuous tense?

options.text: I will finish my work by tomorrow.
options.explanation: This uses the simple future tense, not the future continuous tense.

options.text: I will be finishing my work at this time tomorrow.
options.explanation: This correctly uses the future continuous tense to describe an action in progress at a future time.

options.text: I will have finished my work by tomorrow.
options.explanation: This uses the future perfect tense, not the future continuous tense.

questions.explanation: The future continuous tense ('will be finishing') is used to describe an action that will be in progress at a specific time in the future.
questions.hint: Look for the use of 'will be + verb-ing' to indicate an action in progress at a future time.
questions.subject: ctet-language2

questions.question: Read the following sentence and identify the tense used: 'She had been living in Paris for three years before she moved to London.'

options.explanation: Present perfect continuous tense describes an action that started in the past and continues to the present, not a completed action before another past action.
Past continuous tense describes an action in progress at a specific time in the past, not an action completed before another past action.
Past perfect continuous tense ('had been living') correctly describes an action that started and continued in the past before another past action.

questions.explanation: The sentence describes an action that started in the past, continued for some time, and was completed before another past action, which is the definition of the past perfect continuous tense ('had been living').
questions.hint: Look for the use of 'had been + verb-ing' to indicate an action that started and continued in the past before another past action.
questions.subject: ctet-language2
